solyanka.name: Solyanka
solyanka.summary: A thick, sour soup of Russian origin, common across Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and other former Eastern Bloc countries, and once a staple dish in East Germany.

evapi.name: Ćevapi
evapi.summary: A grilled dish of minced meat popular across Southeast Europe, considered a national dish of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia, often served in flatbread with onions and ajvar.

vierlande.name: Vierlande
vierlande.summary: A roughly 77-square-kilometre farming region within Hamburg, made up of four historic parishes dating to 1556.

altes-land.name: Altes Land
altes-land.summary: Reclaimed marshland region near Hamburg along the Elbe, the largest contiguous fruit-producing area in North Europe, known mainly for apples and cherries.

wilhelmsburg-hamburg.name: Wilhelmsburg
wilhelmsburg-hamburg.summary: A quarter of Hamburg, Germany, situated on islands in the Elbe river, historically known as the city's 'milk isle' before industrialization.

korn-liquor.name: Korn
korn-liquor.summary: German colorless distilled spirit made from grain, usually rye or wheat, distilled to a lower proof and less filtered than vodka so more grain flavor remains.

neuwerk.name: Neuwerk
neuwerk.summary: A small tidal island in the Wadden Sea off the German coast, administratively part of Hamburg, reachable on foot at low tide.

saxony-anhalt.name: Saxony-Anhalt
saxony-anhalt.summary: A German state formed in 1945 from the former Prussian Province of Saxony and the Free State of Anhalt, dissolved in 1952 and re-established after reunification in 1990.

magdeburg-b-rde.name: Magdeburg Börde
magdeburg-b-rde.summary: Fertile loess landscape west and south of Magdeburg, Germany, noted for its rich chernozem soils.

crispbread.name: Crispbread
crispbread.summary: A flat, dry bread made mostly from rye flour that keeps fresh for a long time due to its lack of water, historically considered a poor man's staple food.

bauhaus.name: Bauhaus
bauhaus.summary: A German art and design school founded by Walter Gropius in 1919, combining crafts and fine arts and later closed in 1933 under Nazi pressure, hugely influential in modern design and architecture.

walter-gropius.name: Walter Gropius
walter-gropius.summary: A German-American architect (1883–1969) who founded the Bauhaus school in Weimar in 1919 and became a leading figure of modernist, international-style architecture.

degenerate-art.name: Degenerate Art
degenerate-art.summary: A label the Nazi Party applied to modern art it considered un-German or Jewish, culminating in a 1937 Munich exhibition that mocked confiscated modernist works to turn public opinion against them.

adolf-hitler.name: Adolf Hitler
adolf-hitler.summary: Austrian-born German dictator who led Nazi Germany from 1933 until his suicide in 1945, launching the Second World War and directing the Holocaust.

weimar-republic.name: Weimar Republic
weimar-republic.summary: German state and its first constitutional republic, from 1918 to 1933, formed after Germany's defeat in World War I and ended by the rise of the Nazis.

arnold-schoenberg.name: Arnold Schoenberg
arnold-schoenberg.summary: Austrian-American modernist composer and teacher (1874–1951) who pioneered atonal, twelve-tone music and mentored composers of the Second Viennese School.

paul-hindemith.name: Paul Hindemith
paul-hindemith.summary: German and American composer, music theorist and violist (1895–1963), a leading figure of the New Objectivity style who fled Nazi Germany before World War II.

kurt-weill.name: Kurt Weill
kurt-weill.summary: German-born American composer (1900–1950) best known for collaborating with Bertolt Brecht on The Threepenny Opera; he fled Nazi Germany in 1933 and later wrote for American musical theater.

weimar.name: Weimar
weimar.summary: City in Thuringia, Germany, home to Goethe and Schiller during the German Enlightenment, later a music centre and birthplace of the Bauhaus design movement, and namesake of the Weimar Republic.

thuringia.name: Thuringia
thuringia.summary: A state in central Germany, home to Erfurt and Weimar, whose medieval duchy was founded around 631 CE and which later became a state of the Weimar Republic in 1920.

dessau.name: Dessau
dessau.summary: A city in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, at the meeting of the Mulde and Elbe rivers, now part of Dessau-Roßlau.

november-group-german.name: Novembergruppe
november-group-german.summary: A group of German expressionist artists and architects formed in December 1918, named after the German Revolution, who campaigned for greater artistic influence in schools and law.

erich-mendelsohn.name: Erich Mendelsohn
erich-mendelsohn.summary: German-British architect (1887–1953) known for Expressionist buildings in the 1920s and for pioneering Art Deco and Streamline Moderne design.

einstein-tower.name: Einstein Tower
einstein-tower.summary: An astrophysical observatory in Potsdam, Germany, built in 1924 by architect Erich Mendelsohn to house a solar telescope testing Einstein's relativity theory, and still a working observatory today.

bruno-taut.name: Bruno Taut
bruno-taut.summary: German architect, urban planner and author (1880-1938) active in the Weimar period, known for Expressionist theoretical works and building designs.

hermann-finsterlin.name: Hermann Finsterlin
hermann-finsterlin.summary: German expressionist architect, painter and writer (1887–1973) whose visionary building designs were never built because of harsh economic conditions.

german-revolution-of-1918-1919.name: German Revolution of 1918-19
german-revolution-of-1918-1919.summary: Also called the November Revolution, this uprising toppled the German Empire at the end of World War I and led to the founding of the Weimar Republic.

joseph-goebbels.name: Joseph Goebbels
joseph-goebbels.summary: German politician who served as Nazi chief propagandist and Reich Minister of Propaganda from 1933 until his suicide in 1945, one of Hitler's closest followers.

emil-nolde.name: Emil Nolde
emil-nolde.summary: A German Expressionist painter, born 1867, known for vivid color and brushwork, though also a Nazi Party member with racist views despite his art being labeled 'degenerate' by the regime.

ernst-barlach.name: Ernst Barlach
ernst-barlach.summary: German expressionist sculptor (1870–1938) mostly known for works protesting World War I; the Nazis confiscated much of his art as "degenerate".

erich-heckel.name: Erich Heckel
erich-heckel.summary: German painter and printmaker (1883–1970), a founding member of the group Die Brücke, which existed from 1905 to 1913.

alfred-rosenberg.name: Alfred Rosenberg
alfred-rosenberg.summary: Baltic German Nazi philosopher and convicted war criminal who ran the Nazi Party's foreign affairs office and its cultural policy body, and was executed in 1946 after the Nuremberg trials.

f-hrermuseum.name: Führermuseum
f-hrermuseum.summary: An unbuilt museum Adolf Hitler planned for his hometown of Linz, Austria, to display art bought, confiscated or stolen by the Nazis across Europe during World War II.

linz.name: Linz
linz.summary: Capital of Upper Austria and the country's third-largest city, on the Danube, grown from the Roman settlement of Lentia into a Habsburg commercial centre.

zollverein-coal-mine-industrial-complex.name: Zeche Zollverein
zollverein-coal-mine-industrial-complex.summary: A former coal mine and coking plant complex in Essen, Germany, active from 1851 to 1986, whose 1932 Shaft 12 building earned it fame as the 'most beautiful coal mine in the world.'

fritz-schupp.name: Fritz Schupp
fritz-schupp.summary: German architect (1896-1974) who built 69 factories and plants, best known for designing the Zollverein Coal Mine Industrial Complex, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

hufeisensiedlung.name: Hufeisensiedlung
hufeisensiedlung.summary: A Berlin housing estate built in 1925–33 by architect Bruno Taut and others, later named part of the Berlin Modernism Housing Estates UNESCO World Heritage Site.

walter-farmer.name: Walter Farmer
walter-farmer.summary: A US Army captain (1911–1997) who drafted the Wiesbaden manifesto, leading to the return of much of the artwork the US Army had collected in World War II to its countries of origin.

order-of-merit-of-the-federal-republic-o.name: Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany
order-of-merit-of-the-federal-republic-o.summary: Germany's highest civilian honor, created in 1951 and open to any field; it has gone to over 262,000 people, though annual numbers have fallen sharply since the 1990s.
order-of-merit-of-the-federal-republic-o.source_title: Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany

rudolf-steiner.name: Rudolf Steiner
rudolf-steiner.summary: An Austrian philosopher and esotericist (1861–1925) who founded the spiritual movement anthroposophy and later worked on projects including Waldorf education and biodynamic agriculture.

goetheanum.name: Goetheanum
goetheanum.summary: The world center for the anthroposophical movement in Dornach, Switzerland, designed by Rudolf Steiner; its current building, replacing one lost to fire, was completed in 1928.

geoffrey-roberts.name: Geoffrey Roberts
geoffrey-roberts.summary: A British historian, born in 1952, specializing in Soviet diplomatic and military history of World War II.

eastern-front-world-war-ii.name: Eastern Front
eastern-front-world-war-ii.summary: The World War II theatre fought mainly between Germany and the Soviet Union from 1941 to 1945, where about 30 million of the war's 70 to 85 million deaths occurred and which was decisive in defeating Nazi Germany.

8-8-cm-flak-18-36-37-41.name: 8.8 cm Flak
8-8-cm-flak-18-36-37-41.summary: A German 88mm anti-aircraft and anti-tank gun developed in the 1930s, nicknamed the "eighty-eight," widely feared by Allied troops as a tank killer in World War II.

anschluss.name: Anschluss
anschluss.summary: The annexation of Austria into Nazi Germany on 12 March 1938, driven by decades of support for uniting the two German-speaking states.

sudetenland.name: Sudetenland
sudetenland.summary: Border regions of former Czechoslovakia inhabited mainly by German speakers, annexed by Nazi Germany after the 1938 Sudeten crisis and later returned to Czechoslovakia after World War II.

r-diger-overmans.name: Rüdiger Overmans
r-diger-overmans.summary: A German military historian, born in 1954, known for his study of German military deaths in World War II.

reichswehr.name: Reichswehr
reichswehr.summary: The official German armed forces from 1919 to 1935, limited in size by the Treaty of Versailles until reorganized into the Wehrmacht under Hitler.

anglo-german-naval-agreement.name: Anglo-German Naval Agreement
anglo-german-naval-agreement.summary: A 1935 deal letting Germany build a navy up to 35% the size of Britain's Royal Navy, agreed without consulting France or Italy; Hitler scrapped it in 1939.

edward-wood-1st-earl-of-halifax.name: Lord Halifax
edward-wood-1st-earl-of-halifax.summary: British Conservative politician (1881–1959) who served as Foreign Secretary from 1938 to 1940 and helped shape the policy of appeasing Adolf Hitler.

anglo-polish-alliance.name: Anglo-Polish Agreement
anglo-polish-alliance.summary: A military alliance formalised on 31 March 1939 in which Britain and Poland promised mutual assistance against invasion, especially from Nazi Germany.

richard-overy.name: Richard Overy
richard-overy.summary: British historian (born 1947) known for his work on World War II and Nazi Germany, who in 2007 selected the 50 key dates of world history for The Times.

willy-brandt.name: Willy Brandt
willy-brandt.summary: German politician and chancellor of West Germany from 1969 to 1974, who won the 1971 Nobel Peace Prize for improving relations with Eastern Europe.

warsaw-ghetto-uprising.name: Warsaw Ghetto Uprising
warsaw-ghetto-uprising.summary: A 1943 revolt by Jewish resistance fighters in Nazi-occupied Warsaw against deportation to death camps, the largest single Jewish uprising against the Nazis in World War II.

andr-s-toma.name: András Toma
andr-s-toma.summary: Hungarian soldier captured by the Red Army in 1944 and found living in a Russian psychiatric hospital in 2000, most likely the last World War II prisoner of war to be repatriated, after over 50 years without a conversation.

socialist-realism.name: Socialist realism
socialist-realism.summary: The official art style of the Soviet Union and other socialist states, using idealized, photorealistic scenes to advance the socialist cause; proclaimed doctrine in 1934.

thomas-mann.name: Thomas Mann
thomas-mann.summary: A German novelist (1875–1955) and 1929 Nobel laureate in Literature, known for Buddenbrooks and The Magic Mountain; he fled Nazi Germany in 1933.

hermann-hesse.name: Hermann Hesse
hermann-hesse.summary: German-Swiss poet and novelist (1877–1962) who won the 1946 Nobel Prize in Literature, known for novels like Siddhartha and Steppenwolf on self-discovery.

g-nter-grass.name: Günter Grass
g-nter-grass.summary: German novelist, poet and sculptor (1927–2015) awarded the 1999 Nobel Prize in Literature, best known for his 1959 novel The Tin Drum.

peter-handke.name: Peter Handke
peter-handke.summary: Austrian novelist, playwright and screenwriter awarded the 2019 Nobel Prize in Literature, seen as one of the most influential German-language writers of the late 20th century.

franz-kafka.name: Franz Kafka
franz-kafka.summary: German-language Jewish writer from Prague (1883–1924), a major 20th-century literary figure known for surreal, bureaucratic themes; author of The Metamorphosis, The Trial and The Castle.

the-metamorphosis.name: The Metamorphosis
the-metamorphosis.summary: Franz Kafka's 1915 novella about a salesman who wakes to find himself transformed into a huge insect, one of his best-known works.

the-trial.name: The Trial
the-trial.summary: Franz Kafka's German-language novel, written in 1914–1915 and published posthumously in 1925, about a bank official prosecuted by an inaccessible authority for a crime never revealed to him.

the-castle-novel.name: The Castle
the-castle-novel.summary: Franz Kafka's last novel, published posthumously in 1926, in which a character known only as "K." struggles in vain to reach the mysterious authorities governing a village from its castle.

exilliteratur.name: Exilliteratur
exilliteratur.summary: German for 'exile literature,' works produced by German-speaking writers, many Jewish or anti-Nazi, who fled Germany and Austria between 1933 and 1945.

inner-emigration.name: Innere Emigration
inner-emigration.summary: A concept describing people who feel alienated from their own country's government or culture while still living within it, notably applied to German writers who stayed in Nazi Germany rather than going into exile.

heinrich-b-ll.name: Heinrich Böll
heinrich-b-ll.summary: German writer (1917–1985) considered one of Germany's foremost post-World War II authors, who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1972.

group-47.name: Group 47
group-47.summary: A loose association of German writers convened by Hans Werner Richter from 1947 to 1967 to critique literature and promote new authors after World War II censorship ended.

tr-mmerliteratur.name: Trümmerliteratur
tr-mmerliteratur.summary: A German literary movement, meaning 'rubble literature,' that began after World War II and dealt with returning soldiers confronting the ruin of their homeland and ideals.

paul-celan.name: Paul Celan
paul-celan.summary: German-speaking Romanian poet (1920–1970) and Holocaust survivor who took his pen name after the war and became a French citizen in 1955; regarded as one of the most important post-World War II German-language poets.

thea-von-harbou.name: Thea von Harbou
thea-von-harbou.summary: German screenwriter, novelist, film director and actress (1888–1954), remembered for scripting the classic film Metropolis and writing the 1925 novel it was based on.

metropolis-novel.name: Metropolis (novel)
metropolis-novel.summary: A 1925 German science fiction novel by Thea von Harbou, written as the basis for her and Fritz Lang's 1927 film of the same name.

fritz-lang.name: Fritz Lang
fritz-lang.summary: Austrian-born film director (1890-1976), dubbed the 'Master of Darkness,' best known for the films Metropolis (1927) and M (1931).

perry-rhodan.name: Perry Rhodan
perry-rhodan.summary: A German space opera book series that began in 1961, named after its hero; with about two billion copies sold, it is the best-selling science fiction book series ever.

aufbauliteratur.name: Aufbauliteratur
aufbauliteratur.summary: Literature produced in East Germany between 1949 and 1961 promoting socialist nation-building under the party's "Aufbau des Sozialismus" program.

christa-wolf.name: Christa Wolf
christa-wolf.summary: German novelist and essayist (1929–2011), considered one of the most important writers to emerge from East Germany.

der-geteilte-himmel.name: Divided Sky
der-geteilte-himmel.summary: A 1963 novel by East German writer Christa Wolf, exploring personal integrity within the flawed system of the German Democratic Republic; it won the Heinrich Mann Prize.

soviet-occupation-zone-in-germany.name: Soviet Occupation Zone
soviet-occupation-zone-in-germany.summary: The area of Germany occupied by the Soviet Union after the 1945 Potsdam Agreement, from which East Germany was formally established in 1949.

gy-rgy-luk-cs.name: György Lukács
gy-rgy-luk-cs.summary: Hungarian Marxist philosopher and literary critic (1885–1971), a founder of Western Marxism and influential theorist of literary realism.

willi-bredel.name: Willi Bredel
willi-bredel.summary: German writer (1901–1964) and president of the East German Academy of Arts, a pioneer of socialist realist literature.

ernst-ottwalt.name: Ernst Ottwalt
ernst-ottwalt.summary: Pen name of German communist writer and playwright (1901–1943) who fled Nazi Germany and later died in a Soviet gulag during the Great Purge.

wilhelm-meister-s-apprenticeship.name: Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship
wilhelm-meister-s-apprenticeship.summary: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's second novel (1795–96), a coming-of-age Bildungsroman later held up as a model for literary character development.

johann-wolfgang-von-goethe.name: Goethe
johann-wolfgang-von-goethe.summary: German polymath (1749–1832) widely regarded as the most influential writer in the German language, who also wrote scientific treatises on botany, anatomy and colour and served on the Duke of Weimar's privy council.

galaxy-science-fiction.name: Galaxy Science Fiction
galaxy-science-fiction.summary: An American science fiction magazine published from 1950 to 1980, edited first by H. L. Gold and later Frederik Pohl, known for social-issue stories by writers such as Ray Bradbury.

otto-hahn.name: Otto Hahn
otto-hahn.summary: German chemist (1879–1968) called the father of nuclear chemistry, who co-discovered nuclear fission in 1938 with Lise Meitner and Fritz Strassmann and won the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

lise-meitner.name: Lise Meitner
lise-meitner.summary: Austrian-Swedish physicist (1878–1968) who helped uncover nuclear fission and was the first woman to become a full physics professor in Germany, later ousted by Nazi anti-Jewish laws.

fritz-strassmann.name: Fritz Strassmann
fritz-strassmann.summary: German chemist (1902-1980) who, with Otto Hahn in 1938, identified barium from neutron-bombarded uranium, key evidence for discovering nuclear fission.

operation-paperclip.name: Operation Paperclip
operation-paperclip.summary: US intelligence program that brought over 1,600 German scientists, engineers and technicians, some former Nazi Party members, to America between 1945 and 1959 for postwar military research.

operation-osoaviakhim.name: Operation Osoaviakhim
operation-osoaviakhim.summary: Secret 1946 Soviet operation that took more than 2,500 German scientists, engineers and technicians, plus about 4,000 family members, from occupied Germany to the Soviet Union for research work.

denazification.name: Denazification
denazification.summary: An Allied effort after World War II to remove Nazi Party and SS members from power in Germany and Austria and try prominent Nazis for war crimes, largely abandoned by 1951.

waffenamt.name: Heereswaffenamt
waffenamt.summary: The German Army Weapons Agency, renamed Heereswaffenamt in 1922, responsible for developing, testing and procuring weapons and equipment for the German military through the Nazi era.

bernhard-rust.name: Bernhard Rust
bernhard-rust.summary: Nazi Germany's Minister of Science, Education and National Culture (1883-1945), who issued decrees to immerse German youth in Nazi ideology and also served as party Gauleiter in Hanover and Brunswick from 1925 to 1940.

german-academy-of-sciences-at-berlin.name: German Academy of Sciences at Berlin
german-academy-of-sciences-at-berlin.summary: East Germany's most eminent research institution, a continuation of the Prussian Academy of Sciences, reopened in 1946 and renamed Academy of Sciences of the GDR in 1972 before dissolving in 1992.
german-academy-of-sciences-at-berlin.source_title: German Academy of Sciences at Berlin

reichsforschungsrat.name: Reich Research Council
reichsforschungsrat.summary: A German government body created in 1936 to centrally plan basic and applied research, reorganized in 1942 under the Ministry of Armaments and War Production.

herbert-a-wagner.name: Herbert A. Wagner
herbert-a-wagner.summary: Austrian-American scientist (1900–1982) known for developing the Henschel Hs 293 glide bomb and for work on aircraft aerodynamics and structures.

walther-gerlach.name: Walther Gerlach
walther-gerlach.summary: A German physicist (1889–1979) who in 1922 first demonstrated spin quantization in a magnetic field, the Stern–Gerlach effect, and later served as Nazi Germany's plenipotentiary for nuclear physics until his capture in 1945.

philipp-scheidemann.name: Philipp Scheidemann
philipp-scheidemann.summary: German Social Democratic politician (1865–1939) who proclaimed the German Republic in 1918 and briefly served as the Weimar Republic's Reich Minister President.

charles-i-of-austria.name: Charles I of Austria
charles-i-of-austria.summary: Emperor of Austria and King of Hungary from 1916 to 1918, the last Habsburg monarch of Austria-Hungary, who tried secretly to negotiate peace in World War I before the empire dissolved.

house-of-habsburg.name: Habsburg dynasty
house-of-habsburg.summary: One of Europe's most powerful dynasties, ruling the Holy Roman Empire, Austria and Spain from the Middle Ages until its male line ended in 1740.

kiel.name: Kiel
kiel.summary: The capital of Schleswig-Holstein in northern Germany, a major Baltic Sea port granted city rights in 1242 and long important for shipbuilding and naval activity.

wilhelm-ii.name: Wilhelm II
wilhelm-ii.summary: The last German Emperor, reigning from 1888 until his abdication in 1918, whose provocative policies helped alienate Germany from much of Europe.

paul-von-hindenburg.name: Paul von Hindenburg
paul-von-hindenburg.summary: German military officer and statesman who led the Imperial German Army in World War I and served as President of Germany from 1925 until 1934, appointing Hitler as Chancellor in 1933.

otto-von-habsburg.name: Otto von Habsburg
otto-von-habsburg.summary: Last crown prince of Austria-Hungary (1912–2011) who became pretender to the Habsburg thrones and head of the House of Habsburg-Lorraine after his father's death in 1922.

konrad-adenauer.name: Konrad Adenauer
konrad-adenauer.summary: First chancellor of West Germany (1949–1963) and first leader of the Christian Democratic Union, earlier serving as Mayor of Cologne from 1917 to 1933; considered a founding father of the European Union.

fritz-fischer-historian.name: Fritz Fischer
fritz-fischer-historian.summary: German historian (1908-1999) who argued in the 1960s that Imperial Germany bore sole responsibility for World War I, sparking a major historical debate.

johannes-bell.name: Johannes Bell
johannes-bell.summary: German jurist and politician (1868–1949) who briefly held several ministerial posts and was one of the two German representatives who signed the Treaty of Versailles in 1919.

social-democratic-party-of-germany.name: SPD
social-democratic-party-of-germany.summary: Germany's centre-left Social Democratic Party, founded in 1875, once the largest socialist party in Western Europe until it was banned by the Nazis in 1933.

martin-heidegger.name: Martin Heidegger
martin-heidegger.summary: German philosopher (1889–1976) central to phenomenology, hermeneutics and existentialism, whose 1927 book Being and Time is considered one of modern philosophy's most significant works.

ludwig-wittgenstein.name: Ludwig Wittgenstein
ludwig-wittgenstein.summary: Austro-British philosopher (1889–1951) working in logic and philosophy of language, born into a wealthy Viennese family and educated under Bertrand Russell at Cambridge.

gottlob-frege.name: Gottlob Frege
gottlob-frege.summary: A German philosopher, logician and mathematician (1848–1925) considered the father of analytic philosophy and one of the greatest logicians since Aristotle, though largely ignored in his own lifetime.

edmund-husserl.name: Edmund Husserl
edmund-husserl.summary: An Austrian and German philosopher and mathematician (1859-1938) who founded phenomenology, arguing that consciousness sets the limits of all possible knowledge; barred from his university library under Nazi racial laws in 1933.

vienna-circle.name: Vienna Circle
vienna-circle.summary: A group of philosophers and scientists who met at the University of Vienna from 1924 to 1936, developing logical positivism and greatly influencing philosophy of science.

moritz-schlick.name: Moritz Schlick
moritz-schlick.summary: German philosopher and physicist (1882–1936), founder of logical positivism and leader of the Vienna Circle, murdered by a former student.

karl-jaspers.name: Karl Jaspers
karl-jaspers.summary: German-Swiss psychiatrist and philosopher (1883-1969) whose 1913 work on psychopathology influenced later diagnostic criteria; later seen as a major exponent of existentialism, though he rejected the label.

logical-positivism.name: Logical positivism
logical-positivism.summary: A philosophical movement rooted in empiricism holding that statements are meaningful only if verifiable through observation or true by definition, emerging in the late 1920s Vienna Circle.

herbert-marcuse.name: Herbert Marcuse
herbert-marcuse.summary: German-American philosopher (1898–1979) of the Frankfurt School whose criticism of capitalism and technology made him a leading theorist of the 1960s–70s New Left.

frankfurt-school.name: Frankfurt School
frankfurt-school.summary: A school of sociological and critical-theory thought tied to the Institute for Social Research, founded in 1923, whose thinkers combined Marxism, psychoanalysis and sociology in pursuit of human emancipation.

j-rgen-habermas.name: Jürgen Habermas
j-rgen-habermas.summary: German philosopher and social theorist (1929–2026) associated with the Frankfurt School, known for work on communicative rationality and the public sphere.

rudolf-carnap.name: Rudolf Carnap
rudolf-carnap.summary: A German philosopher and logician (1891–1970), active in Europe before 1935 and the US afterward, a major member of the Vienna Circle and advocate of logical positivism.

otto-neurath.name: Otto Neurath
otto-neurath.summary: Austrian philosopher of science, sociologist and political economist (1882–1945) who invented the ISOTYPE method of pictorial statistics and was a leading figure of the Vienna Circle before fleeing in 1934.

berlin-circle.name: Berlin Circle
berlin-circle.summary: A group of philosophers who held logical empiricist views, closely related to the Vienna Circle.

hans-reichenbach.name: Hans Reichenbach
hans-reichenbach.summary: German philosopher of science (1891–1953) who founded the Berlin Circle in 1928 and championed logical empiricism, writing on probability, relativity and quantum mechanics.

david-hilbert.name: David Hilbert
david-hilbert.summary: A German mathematician (1862–1943) and one of the most influential mathematicians of all time, known for foundational work across many fields and for posing a famous set of problems in 1900.

martin-buber.name: Martin Buber
martin-buber.summary: Austrian-Israeli philosopher (1878–1965) known for his philosophy of dialogue distinguishing "I–Thou" from "I–It" relationships, set out in his 1923 book I and Thou.

i-and-thou.name: I and Thou
i-and-thou.summary: 1923 book by philosopher Martin Buber contrasting an 'I-Thou' and an 'I-It' way of relating to the world, his best-known critique of modern objectification in relationships.

wilhelm-dilthey.name: Wilhelm Dilthey
wilhelm-dilthey.summary: German philosopher (1833–1911) who held Hegel's former chair at the University of Berlin and worked to establish the methodological foundations of history and the human sciences.

georg-simmel.name: Georg Simmel
georg-simmel.summary: German sociologist, philosopher and critic (1858–1918) and a founding figure of sociology, known for pioneering analyses of individuality, social fragmentation and urban life.

lebensphilosophie.name: Lebensphilosophie
lebensphilosophie.summary: A German philosophical movement of the late 19th and early 20th centuries emphasizing life's meaning and value, drawing on Schopenhauer and Nietzsche and influencing later existentialism.

carl-jung.name: Carl Jung
carl-jung.summary: A Swiss psychiatrist and psychotherapist (1875–1961) who founded analytical psychology and is known for his concept of archetypes. Working at Zurich's Burghölzli hospital, he developed an influential friendship and correspondence with Sigmund Freud.

german-collective-guilt.name: Kollektivschuld
german-collective-guilt.summary: A contested idea of shared responsibility attributed to the German people as a whole for the Holocaust and other Nazi-era atrocities.

martin-niem-ller.name: Martin Niemöller
martin-niem-ller.summary: German theologian and Lutheran pastor (1892–1984) who opposed the Nazi regime and was imprisoned in concentration camps from 1938 to 1945, later becoming a vocal pacifist.

stuttgart-declaration-of-guilt.name: Stuttgart Declaration of Guilt
stuttgart-declaration-of-guilt.summary: A 1945 declaration by the Council of the Protestant Church in Germany confessing guilt for its inadequate opposition to the Nazis.

bernhard-schlink.name: Bernhard Schlink
bernhard-schlink.summary: German lawyer, academic and novelist born in 1944, best known for his 1995 international bestseller The Reader; won the 2014 Park Kyong-ni Prize.

turnip-winter.name: Turnip Winter
turnip-winter.summary: A period of severe civilian hardship in Germany over the winter of 1916–1917, when a British naval blockade and poor harvests forced people to rely on turnips as a famine food.

johann-sebastian-bach.name: Johann Sebastian Bach
johann-sebastian-bach.summary: German Baroque composer (1685–1750) known for works such as the Brandenburg Concertos and Goldberg Variations; orphaned at age 10, he is now regarded as one of the greatest composers in Western music.

eisenach.name: Eisenach
eisenach.summary: A town in Thuringia, Germany, an early capital of Thuringia where Martin Luther translated the Bible and where Johann Sebastian Bach was born in 1685.

german-football-association.name: German Football Association
german-football-association.summary: The governing body of football in Germany, a founding member of FIFA and UEFA, overseeing the national leagues and the men's and women's national teams.

weimar-culture.name: Weimar culture
weimar-culture.summary: Flourishing of the arts and sciences in Germany during the Weimar Republic (1918 to 1933), centred on 1920s Berlin and driven heavily by Jewish intellectuals and artists.

schlager-music.name: Schlager
schlager-music.summary: Style of catchy, sentimental European pop music, prominent in early Eurovision Song Contest years and popular through festivals held in Cold War East Germany.

the-tin-drum-film.name: The Tin Drum
the-tin-drum-film.summary: A 1979 West German anti-war film directed by Volker Schlöndorff, adapted from Günter Grass's 1959 novel, about a boy who wills himself to stop growing amid the rise of the Nazis; it won the Palme d'Or and an Academy Award.

nowhere-in-africa.name: Nowhere in Africa
nowhere-in-africa.summary: A 2001 German drama film, based on a 1995 autobiographical novel, about a German-Jewish family that fled to Kenya in 1938 to escape Nazi persecution; it won the 2002 Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film.

the-lives-of-others.name: The Lives of Others
the-lives-of-others.summary: A 2006 German drama about Stasi surveillance of an East Berlin playwright, winner of the 2007 Academy Award for Best International Feature Film.

deutschlandlied.name: Deutschlandlied
deutschlandlied.summary: A German poem and anthem by August Heinrich Hoffmann von Fallersleben; only its third stanza has been Germany's official anthem since reunification in 1991.

gott-strafe-england.name: Gott strafe England
gott-strafe-england.summary: An anti-British slogan meaning 'May God punish England', coined in 1917 by German poet Ernst Lissauer and widely adopted, including by the Imperial German Army.

albert-einstein.name: Albert Einstein
albert-einstein.summary: German-born theoretical physicist (1879–1955) who developed the theory of relativity and won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics.

amiga-record-label.name: Amiga
amiga-record-label.summary: An East German record label founded in 1947, releasing folk, jazz, pop and other music under state ownership before being acquired by Bertelsmann Music Group in 1994.

nina-hagen.name: Nina Hagen
nina-hagen.summary: German singer, songwriter and actress (born 1955), known for her theatrical vocals and rise to prominence in the punk and Neue Deutsche Welle movements, called 'The Godmother of German Punk'.

du-hast-den-farbfilm-vergessen.name: Du hast den Farbfilm vergessen
du-hast-den-farbfilm-vergessen.summary: A 1974 East German pop song, first sung by Nina Hagen, about a girl scolding her boyfriend for forgetting the camera film; widely heard as veiled criticism of drab Eastern Bloc life.

veronika-fischer.name: Veronika Fischer
veronika-fischer.summary: A German singer, also known as Vroni, born in 1951.

otto-von-bismarck.name: Otto von Bismarck
otto-von-bismarck.summary: German statesman (1815–1898) who oversaw the unification of Germany through three wars and served as its first chancellor from 1871 to 1890, known as the "Iron Chancellor."

kulturkampf.name: Kulturkampf
kulturkampf.summary: Seven-year political conflict (1871–1878) between the Catholic Church in Germany and the Kingdom of Prussia under Chancellor Bismarck over control of education and church appointments, marked also by anti-Polish sentiment.

ernst-lissauer.name: Ernst Lissauer
ernst-lissauer.summary: German poet and dramatist (1882–1937) best known for coining the World War I anti-British slogan "Gott strafe England."

john-heartfield.name: John Heartfield
john-heartfield.summary: A German visual artist (1891–1968), born Helmut Herzfeld, who pioneered the use of art as a political weapon through anti-Nazi, anti-fascist photomontages, and co-founded the Malik-Verlag publishing house in 1916.

jaroslav-ha-ek.name: Jaroslav Hašek
jaroslav-ha-ek.summary: A Czech writer and satirist (1883–1923) best known for The Fateful Adventures of the Good Soldier Švejk, a World War I satire on inept authority, translated into about 60 languages.

the-good-soldier-vejk.name: The Good Soldier Švejk
the-good-soldier-vejk.summary: Unfinished satirical novel by Czech writer Jaroslav Hašek (1921–1923) about a good-humored, simple-minded man serving Austria-Hungary in World War I; the most translated Czech novel.

deutscher-fernsehfunk.name: DFF2
deutscher-fernsehfunk.summary: A channel of Deutscher Fernsehfunk, East Germany's state television broadcaster from 1952 to 1991, which served as a propaganda outlet for the ruling Socialist Unity Party.

central_europe-modern-science-011: German Academy of Sciences at Berlin
